ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by Chulalongkorn University's International Review Board (IRB) with the IRB No.0737/65.
All procedures were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and applicable Thai and international regulations governing human research and privacy.
Potential participants were first informed about the study scope and procedures.
Then, 40 mL of fasting (8 hours) blood was collected between 7 and 8 a.m., and participants were given one hour to rest.
Participants were subsequently classified as either having 'No ε4 allele' or having 'At least one ε4 allele' based on the identified sequence variants.
For the WLL, participants are presented with a list of words to learn across multiple trials, and after a short delay of approximately 5 minutes, are asked to recall the word list for the WLR task.
As a sensitivity analysis, MBI participants were stratified according to the presence or absence of co-occurring MCI.

An a priori power analysis for multivariable linear regression, assuming seven predictors, an anticipated explained variance of 15% (R² = .15), and α = .05, indicated that a minimum of 89 participants were required to achieve 80% power.

Additionally, significant group differences were observed in TMSE, CDR-SB, and MBI-C scores, consistent with the clinical characteristics used to define the study group: MCI participants had the lowest TMSE scores and highest CDR-SB scores, whereas MBI participants had the highest MBI-C scores.
All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.

MCI participants were eligible if they had a TMSE score > 23, a CDR-SB score between 0 and 0.5, subjective memory complaints, and were diagnosed by an experienced neuropsychiatrist using the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) and Petersen's Criteria.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The multivariable regression analyses constituted the primary outcome analyses, focusing on quantitative cognitive and behavioral measures rather than categorical diagnoses. Comparison among diagnostic groups was presented as supplementary descriptive analyses to facilitate clinical interpretation, particularly for readers less familiar with dimensional regression approaches. Standardized regression coefficients (β), t-statistics, p-values, and model-fit statistics were reported. Assumptions of the multivariable regression models were evaluated using regression diagnostics. Multicollinearity was assessed using tolerance and variance inflation factor (VIF) values. Normality of residuals was examined using residual histograms and normal probability (P-P) plots of standardized residuals, while homoscedasticity was visually assessed using plots of standardized residuals against standardized predicted values. An a priori power analysis for multivariable linear regression, assuming seven predictors, an anticipated explained variance of 15% (R² = .15), and α = .05, indicated that a minimum of 89 participants were required to achieve 80% power. Given the final sample of 148 participants, the estimated achieved post-hoc power was approximately 97.3%.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .350", "p = .235"), Sentence = c("Although scores were higher in MCI than in MBI, this difference was not statistically significant (p = .350).", "[Insert Figure 2 around here] prevalence did not significantly differ across diagnostic groups (p = .235)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. An a priori power analysis for multivariable linear regression, assuming seven predictors, an anticipated explained variance of 15% (R² = .15), and α = .05, indicated that a minimum of 89 participants were required to achieve 80% power.

All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment.

text.text: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild behavioral impairment (MBI) are overlapping prodromal states associated with dementia risk.
Circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) may be linked to cognitive and behavioral changes, but their relationships remain unclear.
Examine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos in prodromal dementia.
This cross-sectional study included 148 Thai participants aged 60-75 years: 56 cognitively normal controls, 47 with MCI without MBI, and 45 with MBI with or without MCI.
We measured ApoA1, ApoA2, ApoB, ApoC1, ApoC3, ApoD, ApoE, ApoH, and ApoJ, five lipids, and APOE genotype, and computed an atherogenic Apo composite (ApoB-ApoC1-ApoC3).
Primary analyses used multivariable linear regression of quantitative cognitive and behavioral outcomes.
Group comparisons were secondary and served to contextualize the dimensional regression findings.

Across Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) models, 20.7-28.2% of variance was explained by combinations of ApoH, ApoC3, APOE ε4 carrier status, age, and male sex (inverse associations), and free cholesterol and education (positive associations).

The atherogenic composite was inversely associated with MoCA total, memory index, and delayed recall scores, . and with Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) verbal fluency and word list recall.
No significant predictors emerged for Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) scores or NPI caregiver distress.
All nine Apos differed significantly between groups, with levels highest in MCI, intermediate in MBI, and lowest in controls.
Circulating Apo profiles differed across controls, MCI, and MBI groups and were more consistently associated with cognitive than behavioral outcomes.
ApoH and the atherogenic Apo composite warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of early cognitive dysfunction.
Global aging brings increased risk, prevalence, and public-health burden of dementia, a syndrome characterized by progressive cognitive decline and behavioral changes.

As neurodegeneration involves complex interactions across multiple biological systems, current interventions cannot reliably reverse or halt the underlying pathology once dementia has manifested. 1 With this limitation, early diagnosis and prevention are key in dementia research.

text.text: Among the biomarkers, circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) are plausible candidate markers of dementia-related risk and pathology.

Apos are a group of specialized, multifunctional amphipathic proteins responsible for the stabilization and regulated transport of lipoproteins by binding to lipid surfaces, with different Apo species playing distinct biological roles. 22, 23 Their relevance to dementia is supported by reported associations with neurodegeneration and cognitive function. [24] [25] [26] [27] To date, previous work has explored the role of circulating Apos in cognitive impairment; however, their relationship with MBI remains largely unexplored.

text.text: Circulating ApoE has been the most extensively studied species in dementia, and its concentrations may provide information beyond APOE genotype.

In a population study of over 76,000 individuals, lower plasma ApoE was associated with AD and all-cause dementia independent of APOE genotype and cardiovascular risk factors. 28 Neuropathological work on amygdalae specimens from dementia cases has also demonstrated ApoE enrichment and colocalization with complement component C4 in amyloid plaques, including among individuals without APOE ε4. 29 Longitudinally, lower plasma ApoE in MCI was associated with subsequent progression to AD, poorer cognition, and adverse amyloid, tau, and neurofilament light chain profiles. 30 Research in other Apo species is more heterogeneous and varies by clinical population and biospecimen.

text.text: Two meta-analyses reported lower circulating ApoA1 levels in AD than in controls, 27, 31 whereas an inverse relationship between ApoA1 and cognition was observed in a type 2 diabetes cohort with cognitive impairment. 32 Higher CSF ApoB has been associated with early tau dysregulation and subsequent visuospatial decline, 33 while higher plasma ApoC3 and ApoJ have been linked to higher baseline cognitive function or lower dementia risk in longitudinal studies. 25, 34 Multi-Apo profiling has also identified lower ApoA1, ApoA2, and ApoH, but higher ApoE, ApoJ, and ApoB/ApoA1 ratios in MCI individuals that seemed to correspond with cognitive performance, dementia risk, and brain structure changes. 26 Despite research interests in Apos and cognitive impairment, the available body of knowledge remains inconsistent in establishing circulating Apos as reliable biomarkers of dementia risk. 11 Direct evidence concerning circulating Apo profiles in MBI remains limited, as previous studies have focused primarily on APOE genotype. 35, 36 The present study therefore aimed to examine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos and conventional lipid measures in individuals with MCI without MBI and individuals with MBI with or without co-occurring MCI, compared to controls.

text.text: By analyzing these profiles across participant groups, we sought to clarify whether specific Apo species or composites, along with other demographic factors, are associated with early cognitive or behavioral impairment that could potentially serve as additional candidate correlates of pre-dementia risk.
This cross-sectional study recruited 148 older adults aged 60-75 years from King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital (KCMH), the Thai Red Cross Society, and community-based senior groups in Thailand.

The sample comprised 56 cognitively normal healthy controls who exhibited cognitive and behavioral performance within the normative range, 47 participants with MCI without MBI, and 45 individuals with MBI with (25) or without (20) co-occurring MCI.

Controls were included in the study if they did not meet the study criteria for MCI or Exclusion criteria included dementia; major neurological disorders other than the conditions under study, including multiple sclerosis and stroke; lifetime and current major depressive, bipolar, psychotic, or substance-use disorders; neurodevelopmental disorders; diagnosis of medical disorders such as chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and thyroid disorders; abnormal liver and kidney blood tests; and cognitive training within the previous three months.
Participant screening.
Potential participants were first informed about the study scope and procedures.

Those who remained interested then completed screening assessments, namely the TMSE, CDR-SB, IQCODE, and MBI-C. For individuals with existing hospital medical records, their physicians were contacted to discuss and confirm their neuropsychiatric diagnoses.
For those without prior neuropsychiatric examination or hospital records, an appointment with an experienced neuropsychiatrist was arranged to confirm eligibility before enrollment.
Data collection procedure.
Data were collected between June 2024 and October 2025 at KCMH over one or two visits, depending on participant availability and ability.
After written consent, sociodemographic, medical, medication, and supplement histories were recorded.
Then, 40 mL of fasting (8 hours) blood was collected between 7 and 8 a.m., and participants were given one hour to rest.
Participants then returned for neuropsychological and behavioral testing.
Participants could take breaks between each assessment as needed and were compensated after protocol completion.
Informants were contacted and interviewed within one week of the participant visit.
Blood.
Following collection, fasting blood samples were immediately transported to the hospital laboratory for processing.
Samples were centrifuged and separated into whole blood, serum, and plasma fractions.
Then, some samples were sent to the relevant laboratories for immediate analysis, whilst the rest were stored at -80 o C until thawed for further analysis.

High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), total cholesterol, and triglyceride concentrations were measured in the hospital laboratory using the Alinity C system (Abbott Laboratories, USA; Otawara-Shi, Tochigi-Ken, Japan) with enzymatic, accelerator-selective detergent, and glycerol phosphate oxidase methods, respectively.
The coefficients of variation (CV) were 2.6% for HDL-C, 2.3% for total cholesterol, and 2.3% for triglycerides.
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) was estimated using the Friedewald equation.
Plasma free cholesterol levels were determined using the Free Cholesterol Assay Kit (Catalog #E-BC-K004-M, Elabscience, Houston, TX, USA) according to the manufacturer's protocol.

Based on prespecified biological classifications, ApoA1, ApoE, and ApoJ were grouped as the reputedly protective composite because of their reported antioxidant and antiinflammatory functions. [37] [38] [39] ApoB, ApoC1, and ApoC3 were grouped as the reputedly atherogenic Apo composite due to their reported proatherogenic or inflammatory associations. 40- 42 The remaining species, ApoA2, ApoD, and ApoH, were deemed to have more contextdependent biological roles and were considered separately.

text.text: The ApoB-ApoA1, atherogenicprotective Apo, LDL-C-HDL-C, and triglyceride-HDL-C indices were calculated as differences between the standardized Z-scores of their respective components.
APOE genotyping.
Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using the TIANamp Genomic DNA Kit (TIANGEN Biotech, Beijing, China), according to the manufacturer's instructions.
DNA concentration and purity were assessed before downstream analysis.
The target region of the APOE gene was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the PCR products were examined by agarose gel electrophoresis.
Participants were subsequently classified as either having 'No ε4 allele' or having 'At least one ε4 allele' based on the identified sequence variants.

The MoCA is a highly sensitive, widely validated tool for detecting MCI and early AD. 43 The test comprises 30 total points that determine the individual's performance across eight cognitive domains: visuospatial function, executive function, memory, naming, language, attention, abstraction, and orientation.

text.text: In addition to the total score, MoCA subdomain scores can help further differentiate individuals into distinct cognitive syndromes, 44 whilst the Memory Index Score (MoCA-MIS), a recall score for the memory items, may help further discriminate between normal cognition and MCI 45 and indicate the extent of disease progression.

text.text: Neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia were comprehensively assessed using the NPI, a validated informant-based interview. 47 The tool assesses ten behavioral and two neurovegetative areas: delusions, hallucinations, agitation/aggression, depression/dysphoria, anxiety, elation/euphoria, apathy/indifference, disinhibition, irritability/lability, aberrant motor behavior, sleep and nighttime behavior disorders, and appetite and eating disorders.

text.text: For each domain, informants first indicate whether symptoms are present.
For any present symptom, frequency (1-4), severity (1-3), and associated caregiver distress (0-5) levels are rated.
Frequency and severity scores are then multiplied and summed to produce a total NPI score, whilst caregiver distress scores are summed to give a total caregiver distress score.
The Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) neuropsychological battery.

The CERAD neuropsychological battery comprises standardized cognitive tests designed to assess cognitive function and supports the evaluation of AD and dementia progression. [48] [49] [50] Our study focused on three subtests: verbal fluency (VF), word list learning (WLL), and word list recall (WLR).

text.text: In the VF task, participants have to name as many animals as possible in one minute.
For the WLL, participants are presented with a list of words to learn across multiple trials, and after a short delay of approximately 5 minutes, are asked to recall the word list for the WLR task.
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 32 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) and graphs were generated using MATLAB version R2026b (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA).
Continuous variables were examined for normality using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk test, and are presented as mean (± SD) or median (interquartile range), as appropriate.
Categorical variables are presented as number (percentage).
Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

text.text: There were no missing data for the variables included in the primary analyses.

The study population was selected to encompass a broad spectrum of cognitive and behavioral functioning, including cognitively normal individuals and participants meeting conventional criteria for MCI or MBI.

Rather than treating these diagnostic categories as the principal outcomes, we focused on continuous measures of the cognitive and behavioral phenome. 51, 52 Accordingly, multivariable linear regression was the primary analytical approach, while comparisons between diagnostic groups served a secondary purpose, providing clinical context and facilitating comparisons with existing literature.

text.text: For each analyte, Z-scores were calculated using SPSS based on the entire sample.
Composite values were calculated as the sum of the corresponding component Z-scores, with each component equally weighted.

Z-score standardization eliminated differences in measurement units and concentration scales, ensuring each Apo or lipid contributed equally in terms of standardized variability and preventing analytes with larger absolute concentrations or variances from disproportionately influencing the composite indices.
Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the nine Apos to determine whether a common underlying dimension could be extracted.
Sampling adequacy and the suitability of the correlation matrix for PCA were assessed using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure and Bartlett's test of sphericity, respectively.

The first principal component (PC1) was considered acceptable when the KMO value exceeded 0.70, Bartlett's test was significant (p < .05), PC1 explained more than 50% of the total variance, and all nine Apos showed loadings greater than .70.

text.text: One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to compare continuous variables among groups, while pairwise comparisons were examined with Bonferroni-adjusted contrasts.
When the homogeneity-of-variance assumption was not met, Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post hoc comparisons were used.
Categorical variables were compared using Pearson's chi-square test, while individual NPI symptom frequencies were compared using two-sided Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests.
Apo and lipid concentration differences between groups were examined using general linear models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and metabolic-syndrome status.
Estimated marginal means, 95% confidence intervals, and omnibus tests were reported.

To account for multiple testing across related biomarker outcomes, Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) p-value correction was applied separately within four prespecified families: nine individual apolipoproteins, five individual lipid measures, four derived Apo measures, and two derived lipid measures.
As a sensitivity analysis, MBI participants were stratified according to the presence or absence of co-occurring MCI.
Apo levels were compared between MBI-only and MBI with co-occurring MCI participants using general linear models with age and BMI as covariates and sex and metabolic-syndrome status as fixed factors.
BH-FDR correction was applied across the nine apolipoprotein comparisons.
Multivariable linear regression was used to examine associations with cognitive and global behavioral outcomes.

For each outcome, one model evaluated individual Apo species together with lipid, demographic, and APOE variables, and an alternative model replaced individual Apo candidates with the prespecified composites (protective and atherogenic composites) together with the remaining candidate predictors.
The multivariable regression analyses constituted the primary outcome analyses, focusing on quantitative cognitive and behavioral measures rather than categorical diagnoses.

Comparison among diagnostic groups was presented as supplementary descriptive analyses to facilitate clinical interpretation, particularly for readers less familiar with dimensional regression approaches.
Standardized regression coefficients (β), t-statistics, p-values, and model-fit statistics were reported.
Assumptions of the multivariable regression models were evaluated using regression diagnostics.
Multicollinearity was assessed using tolerance and variance inflation factor (VIF) values.

Normality of residuals was examined using residual histograms and normal probability (P-P) plots of standardized residuals, while homoscedasticity was visually assessed using plots of standardized residuals against standardized predicted values.

An a priori power analysis for multivariable linear regression, assuming seven predictors, an anticipated explained variance of 15% (R² = .15), and α = .05, indicated that a minimum of 89 participants were required to achieve 80% power.
Given the final sample of 148 participants, the estimated achieved post-hoc power was approximately 97.3%.

text.text: The groups did not differ significantly in age, sex distribution, BMI, metabolic-syndrome prevalence, or APOE ε4-carrier status.

Years of education and IQCODE scores differed significantly across groups, with adjusted pairwise comparisons indicating differences between controls and MCI, but not between MBI and either the controls or MCI.

Additionally, significant group differences were observed in TMSE, CDR-SB, and MBI-C scores, consistent with the clinical characteristics used to define the study group: MCI participants had the lowest TMSE scores and highest CDR-SB scores, whereas MBI participants had the highest MBI-C scores.

text.text: This finding suggests that a coordinated increase in circulating Apos may be a shared biological feature of MCI and MBI, potentially reflecting common underlying mechanisms regulating Apo metabolism.

In the multivariable models, ApoH, ApoC3, and the atherogenic Apo composite were inversely associated with selected cognitive outcomes, whilst no candidate predictors were retained for the global neuropsychiatric symptom or caregiver distress measures.

These findings indicate that circulating Apo profiles may be more consistently associated with cognitive performance than with global behavioral burden, though this does not exclude possible associations with individual symptoms or changes over time.

Although the primary outcome variables in this study were continuous measures of cognitive and behavioral functioning, rather than the categorical diagnoses of MCI and MBI, it is notable that both MCI and MBI displayed distinct, but partially overlapping clinical profiles.

MCI was characterized predominantly by poorer cognitive performance, particularly in learning and delayed recall, concurrently with certain behavioral symptoms, whereas MBI was characterized by greater neuropsychiatric burden and caregiver distress, alongside accompanying cognitive deficits.

However, unlike cognitive deficits that may more directly reflect underlying cognitive dysfunction, behavioral symptoms may also be influenced by psychosocial circumstances and environmental factors, 53 and in some cases, may be more closely related to these contextual influences than to the degree of cognitive impairment.

text.text: We found that MCI and MBI share increased circulating Apo levels, although these alterations were associated with cognitive dysfunction rather than behavioral symptom severity or caregiver distress.
Direct evidence relating circulating Apos to MBI is particularly sparse.
Available findings suggest that Apo-behavior associations may vary according to Apo species, symptom domain, and follow-up interval.

In a longitudinal study with cognitive impairment, higher ApoA1 was associated with a lower likelihood of apathy, higher ApoA2 was related to higher prevalence of apathy, higher ApoB and ApoC1 predicted subsequent neuropsychiatric symptoms at two years, higher ApoE was related to fewer symptoms at two years, higher ApoH was associated with anxiety, and higher ApoJ was related to higher prevalence of neuropsychiatric symptoms at one year. 59 This heterogeneous pattern suggests that individual behavioral domains and longitudinal changes may be more informative than a single global symptom score.

text.text: Evidence concerning APOE genotype is similarly mixed.

The coordinated pattern suggests that MCI was accompanied by a broad alteration in circulating Apos rather than an isolated change in a single species.
Direct comparison with previous research is limited because multi-Apo profiles have not, to our knowledge, been examined across the same groups as this work.

Previous studies have reported associations in the opposite direction, with positive relationships between ApoH and global cognitive, memory, or visuospatial performance. 26, 77 Differences in population characteristics, cognitive measures, metabolic status, and laboratory procedures may contribute to this inconsistency.

text.text: Apart from ApoH, ApoC3 showed a more selective pattern, with negative associations with MoCA delayed recall and CERAD verbal fluency.

text.text: Several limitations should be addressed.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes insight into temporal sequence, causality, and prognostic value.
Second, this Thai cohort was predominantly female and relatively highly educated, which may limit generalizability.
The MBI group also included participants with and without co-occurring MCI, whereas the MCI group excluded MBI.
Diagnostic classifications of MCI and MBI represent operationally defined, partly overlapping clinical constructs with potentially limited reliability and substantial withingroup heterogeneity.

Therefore, our regression analyses deliberately focused on quantitative cognitive (MoCA and CERAD) and behavioral (NPI) measures rather than categorical diagnosis, thereby preserving dimensional information and avoiding potentially artificial diagnostic boundaries.
Third, the low frequency of several individual neuropsychiatric symptoms may limit domain-specific behavioral modeling.

Fourth, the multivariable analyses were conducted within the original sample; therefore, the reproducibility and generalizability of the findings require validation in independent cohorts across different countries and cultural settings.
Future studies should use longitudinal cohorts with repeated Apo measurements that are examined alongside established neurodegenerative biomarkers, metabolic and vascular measures, and neuroimaging.

Further internal validation and external replication are needed to evaluate whether ApoH, ApoC3, and the atherogenic Apo composite provide reproducible information about cognitive performance beyond established demographic factors, APOE genotype, and conventional lipid measures.

Emerging novel analytes such as ApoM may also extend the current panel and give rise to different patterns of association, as higher plasma ApoM has been reported in AD than in controls after adjustment for established risk factors. 99

text.text: In this cross-sectional case-control study of Thai older adults, MCI and MBI were characterized by distinct, but partially overlapping, cognitive and behavioral profiles.

Adjusted circulating concentrations of all measured Apo species showed a consistent pattern of highest values in MCI, intermediate in the heterogeneous MBI group, and lowest values in controls, with significant diagnostic-group effects remaining after BH-FDR correction.
ApoH, ApoC3, and the atherogenic Apo composite were inversely associated with certain cognitive measures.
No candidate predictors were retained for global neuropsychiatric symptom or caregiver distress regression models.

These exploratory findings suggest that Apo profiles may be more consistently related to cognitive performance than behavioral severity; however, further studies are required to validate these findings before diagnostic or prognostic utility of the notable Apos can be inferred.
